meta_description: Does your child always insist, "I'll do it myself!"? How do you help them discover the joy of working together? Here's a storybook about the joy of cooperation, plus a role-sharing game you can play at home.

content.alt: 37. Better Together, More Fun! - The child who only cries "I'll do it myself!"
content.text:
The child who only cries "I'll do it myself!"

Blocks, drawings, anything at all—when your child pushes a friend's hand away and insists on doing everything alone, it's easy to worry. But at this age, that "I want to do it myself" feeling is also a natural sign of growing independence.

Still, insisting on doing everything alone can make a child miss out on the joy of doing things together. In moments like these, it helps to first let them feel, through a story, that "doing it together was even better."

Curious about the plot of this cooperation storybook? We take a look at the lessons of the cooperation storybook through pictures. Meet the key scenes of the cooperation storybook's story, too. Read the cooperation storybook together with your child and talk about it. We've gathered all kinds of stories about "37. Better Together, More Fun!"—including sharing storybooks, taking-turns storybooks, and friendship storybooks.
content.caption: Wanting to do it alone is a natural sign that independence is growing.

content.alt: 37. Better Together, More Fun! - Why the joy of cooperation matters
content.text:
Why the joy of cooperation matters

The experience of accomplishing something together grows both a child's social skills and their problem-solving ability. In the process of sharing roles, giving and receiving help, and celebrating the result together, a child learns the feeling of "we."

Cooperation isn't about giving up what's yours—it's the wisdom of achieving together what you can't do alone. As this experience builds up, a child grows stronger in friendships and in learning alike.
content.caption: Cooperation is the wisdom of achieving together what you can't do alone.

content.alt: 37. Better Together, More Fun! - Hori's story of building alone and tumbling down
content.text:
Hori's story of building alone and tumbling down

In Better Together, More Fun!, Hori insists on building the biggest castle in the world all by himself. But he can't reach the top, and it comes crashing down three times, leaving him near tears.

That's when his friends reach out. Kongi carries the blocks, Bori makes the base sturdy, and Toto handles the high spots! When all four join forces, they finish a castle that no one could have built alone. Hori shouts, "Together is a hundred times more fun than alone!" In this scene, a child feels the joy of togetherness right in their heart.
content.caption: He learned that together is a hundred times more fun than alone.

content.alt: 37. Better Together, More Fun! - A role-sharing game to play together at home
content.text:
A role-sharing game to play together at home

Cooperation can be learned through play at home, too. When building blocks or tidying up toys, try sharing roles: "You take the red blocks, Daddy takes the blue ones." When you finish together, it's nice to share the joy: "We did it so fast because we worked together!"

When your child is struggling alone, instead of jumping in to help, try asking, "Would you like some help?" They naturally learn that asking for help—and receiving it—is nothing to be embarrassed about.
content.caption: Learn the joy of sharing roles and finishing together at home, too.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions

Q. How do I teach my child to cooperate?

A. Let them experience through play that doing things together is more fun and works out better. When they feel how much more enjoyable togetherness is compared to going it alone, a cooperative spirit grows naturally.

Q. How does a cooperation storybook help?

A. Watching the characters join forces to accomplish something, a child learns the value of togetherness. A cooperation storybook shows that helping one another lets you achieve bigger things.

Q. My child finds it hard to team up with friends.

A. Try games where each child takes on a role and completes something together. When you celebrate big once you've finished as a group, your child remembers the joy of cooperation with their whole body.
